body:
Adding a field to a database document shouldn’t also be a decision about what users can see in their browsers.

With our frontend listening directly to Firestore, it could be. The browser received whole documents, permissions had to stay synchronized between Firestore rules and our Go backend, and features that needed data from other databases ran into those boundaries. We needed the backend to decide what each user received and keep that decision up to date as both the data and their permissions changed. At millions of live subscriptions, we also needed to do it efficiently.

That led us to build Lovable Realtime, our own realtime service.

I built the core in 40 hands-on working days, and we rolled it out to every user without a single user-facing incident. The service handles peaks of over 2 million concurrent subscriptions and delivers around 2.6 billion data and patch frames per month.

We needed three things together: support for our existing databases, backend-shaped payloads, and reactive authorization. The alternatives either required changing our database stack or left substantial parts of that framework for us to build. Here’s how we evaluated those trade-offs, built the service, and tested the migration before switching users over.

## Challenges with Firestore

Historically, parts of Lovable handled real-time updates by opening Firestore onSnapshot listeners straight from the browser. This has a few problems. It creates two authorization paths: Firestore rules were a mirror of our API’s permissions model in Golang, and we constantly had to remember to keep them in sync. In addition, the browser reads the entire Firestore document on each call. Anyone adding a field to the database is deciding what is exposed to the browser, while not necessarily knowing it. This was a latent but serious risk.

Finally, Firestore’s authorization rules are limited in that they can only query Firebase data. This was a blocker for us when we set out to enable authorization updates for large groups (e.g., the ability to give everyone in your company’s engineering group access to a project). Enterprises use our SCIM feature that syncs users and groups to their Lovable workspace. Features like SCIM need large DB transactions and complex query patterns, which document DBs such as Firestore traditionally do not provide to the same level of a solution like Spanner. But Firestore Security Rules can’t read Spanner.

We rolled out a temporary workaround: proxying onSnapshot subscriptions through our Go API only for businesses and enterprises. This reused the API’s permission system, but the proxy opened separate Firestore listeners for each client’s data dependencies.

At millions of live subscriptions, this would mean maintaining millions of long-lived upstream streams, often watching the same data repeatedly. Those streams also consumed capacity in the API’s shared Firestore connection pool, competing with ordinary database requests. A separate pool would isolate that contention, but would not solve the per-client listener growth. We knew this was a temporary fix and began searching for a new solution.

## Requirements & options considered

As we looked to move away from Firestore, we had three main requirements. First, our data was in Firestore and Spanner and we didn’t want to migrate to a new primary database—the solution would need to work with the data stores we already had (and allow us to add new ones over time). Second, we need authorization to be re-evaluated continuously; it should be able to change while a connection is open and a revoked user’s stream should close mid-session. And third, the backend needs to control the permissions and shape the payload in server code; fields a caller lacks permission for should never leave the server.

We found options for each requirement, but none of the solutions we evaluated met all three requirements while working with our existing data store and Go backend.

Transport services such as Ably, Pusher, PubNub, and Centrifugo provide connections, delivery, and revocation mechanisms. We would still need to build change detection, affected-subscription tracking, and authorized projections.

Replicache lets us bring our own backend: a notification prompts the client to pull, and the server computes its authorized view. We would still need to implement notification routing, server-side views, and change tracking, including changes to the payload caused solely by permission changes.

Database-integrated systems such as Firestore, Firebase RTDB, Supabase Realtime, Hasura, PowerSync, and Zero offer different combinations of live queries, projections, and authorization within their supported stacks. We needed a database-agnostic layer over our existing Firestore and Spanner data, with results computed in our Go backend and access re-evaluated when authorization dependencies change. These products did not provide that combination without substantial integration work.

Electric syncs subsets of Postgres data to clients. Using it would have meant moving or replicating our Firestore and Spanner data into Postgres, rather than building directly on our existing stores.

Meteor’s publications shape per-user payloads in server code, with reactivity centered on MongoDB. Permission dependencies read separately from the reactive data need explicit handling. Convex is close to what we wanted: a server function becomes a reactive, server-shaped subscription, but it requires using Convex’s database.

We built the framework that connects data dependencies, permission changes, and backend-computed subscription results, without moving our data to a new store.

## What we built

Lovable Realtime is a dedicated WebSocket service that streams live data, with authorization and data shape handled server-side in Go.
